examiner_questions.question: Your guide was built on four pillars that your findings overturned. Didn't the guide steer your participants?
examiner_questions.model_answer: The guide asked about trust because the field did; that's where I started, and I quote the headings word for word in 3.3 as evidence of it. But I didn't analyse the data under those headings. The later codings were made against the working claim and then the five-concept codebook, and each had to record the evidence against as well as for. Where I raised a theme myself, like brand, I counted it as declined, not as support: I raised brand in five interviews and it was declined in all five.

examiner_questions.question: Why did you use two instruments, a guide and a script?
examiner_questions.model_answer: The fourteen-question guide is the one the ethics committee approved. The twenty-three-prompt script sat beside it so the conversation could follow the participant rather than the headings. That's the semi-structured form Brinkmann and Kvale describe: the themes are fixed, and the order and follow-up are left to the conversation (3.3).

examiner_questions.question: You planned 45 to 60 minutes, but many interviews were shorter. Does that weaken the data?
examiner_questions.model_answer: They ran from eight minutes to seventy-four, with a median of forty-three, and sixteen of the twenty-six ran forty minutes or more. Fourteen closed sooner than planned, most because the person had said what they came to say. The shortest, A5, is eight minutes of prepared answers, and the coding files flag it, so no finding rests on it.

examiner_questions.question: How did you find your participants?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Purposively, for the kinds of party the question needed, through the projects and publications in which they'd done the work. Then by referral: the script's ninth stage asks who else I should hear. I started chains from each of the three kinds of party, in eleven countries, to limit the bias that referrals run along one person's network (3.3).

examiner_questions.question: Your application promised correlation and regression on the survey. Why didn't you run them?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Because the sample selected itself through my networks, and a self-selected sample supports no estimate beyond itself, as Fowler says. So I read the survey descriptively, for scale, in counts and cross-tabulations, and run no test of significance. The plan is reproduced in C.1 so anyone can see what was promised, and the change is recorded in 3.6 and in Table 3.8 as change 2.

The form opened on 22 February 2024 on the draft's questions as my supervisors approved them, and it ran until 30 April 2025, beside the interviews. So it asks about the four pillars, not the five links, and no link of the chain rests on it.

examiner_questions.question: Approval came the same day you submitted. Was the review adequate?
examiner_questions.model_answer: It went through the Faculty's postgraduate research ethics process and was approved as Category A by the Chair of the School's ethics committee, with a condition that my supervisors approve the final questions before data collection, which was done. The record is the Chair's comment in the University's virtual learning environment, reproduced in C.2 with the Chair's name redacted (C.3).

examiner_questions.question: Your record doesn't list the 72 papers or say why 23 were dropped. How can we trust the 49?
examiner_questions.model_answer: The 2023 record does have gaps, and I set them out myself in E.2.9. The screening log gives 72 as a count and nothing else. The manuscript I submitted to MDPI Future Transportation in March 2023 gives the same counts and four topic labels for what was dropped, crowd-shipping, travelling salesman problems, bicycle deliveries and public transport sharing, but no list of the 72 and no reason per paper. So in 2026 I re-ran that stage: every paper that could have been among the 23, the 30 in the January 2023 EndNote export that aren't in the 49, plus Kanter, coded twice against the 2023 criteria. Twenty-nine exclusions stand, two papers meet the criteria, and neither is a kind the 49 lack. Agreement on subject was 30 of 31, alpha .91 (E.2.10).

examiner_questions.question: Why do you report 860 records when the stages start from 662?
examiner_questions.model_answer: 860 is the 662 records plus the 198 published before 2018. The eight pre-2018 papers I added by hand sit in both, under 'Extra' in the 662 and in the pre-2018 column, so 860 counts them twice. I keep 860 because it's the figure the 2023 manuscript reports, and I explain the double count in E.2.4, in 2.1 and in Table 3.3.

examiner_questions.question: Why did you switch from four databases to OpenAlex for the update?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Reproducibility. The criterion I couldn't do without was that a reader can run the search again. A public index through a public interface allows that for anyone; four databases behind institutional logins allow it only for subscribers. On Culbert and colleagues' comparison OpenAlex's coverage is comparable to Web of Science and Scopus, though it carries fewer abstracts, so every doubtful record got a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).

examiner_questions.question: Can you really compare 241 papers with 49 studies?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Only with care, and I say which kind each is every time they stand together. The 49 were included after full-text reading; the 241 were kept after title-and-abstract screening and the thirty-citation rule, and 170 of them were then read in full. So it's a looser set beside a stricter one (2.2, 3.2).

examiner_questions.question: Your counts on 'where the power sits' look circular.
examiner_questions.model_answer: They are, in part, and I say so. Thirty-eight of the 241 verdicts on power were assigned by a rule that counts shippers, receivers, cities or a neutral orchestrator as support and carriers as against, which is the thesis's own claim. So that count only shows whom the field assumes decides. Whether power really sits there is tested in 4.5, with the interviews and who began the 117 arrangements (2.2; E.3.2.1).

examiner_questions.question: Why did the 2022 string miss the horizontal-collaboration literature?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Because it requires 'last mile'. A paper that says 'horizontal collaboration' but not 'last mile' is invisible to it. Run again in OpenAlex it returns none of the twelve papers in Appendix F, and only 39 of the 231 update papers that weren't in the 2023 review; 192 fall outside its terms altogether (2.2).

examiner_questions.question: How did you choose these twelve? Isn't that cherry-picking?
examiner_questions.model_answer: They're the papers inside the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration, named in the evidence I assembled for the research gap on 15 September 2026. They're not offered as a sample; they're a test of the 2022 string's reach, and run again in OpenAlex it finds none of them. The update itself was then run systematically, with six strings (E.2.8; 2.2).

examiner_questions.question: Three of them aren't about freight. Why include them?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Each names horizontal collaboration, coordination or coopetition in its title, but none is about freight, so a last-mile string couldn't be expected to find them. examiner_questions.question: You interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim. Isn't the analysis just you agreeing with yourself?
examiner_questions.model_answer: That's the exposure no procedure removes, and I name it in 3.7. What I did about it: the second and third codings were made from the transcripts alone, without the notes of the first; each had to record the evidence against as well as for; each half was read a second time without sight of its first codes; and the second coding threw out two of my own clauses, brand and size.

examiner_questions.question: Why report raw agreement rather than kappa?
examiner_questions.model_answer: With four possible stances, thirteen transcripts a half and a fifth concept where silence dominates, a coefficient would say less than the list of the eighteen differences itself. So I give 112 of 130, 86 per cent, and every difference by concept and transcript in Table 3.6. For the 117 arrangements, where the unit and the numbers suit it, I use Krippendorff's alpha.

examiner_questions.question: Did you plant the brand idea in your participants' heads?
examiner_questions.model_answer: I raised it in five interviews and it was declined in all five; participants raised it unprompted in eight. examiner_questions.model_answer: A9 is substantially incomplete and its answers were typed in afterwards, so I read it as low confidence throughout. A5 is eight minutes of prepared answers. B8 has phone audio and limited English. B10 and B11 turned out to lie outside the domain: they stay in every count of twenty-six, both codings mark them silent on most concepts, and no finding rests on them alone (3.7; 4.1).

examiner_questions.question: With a self-selected sample and no response rate, what is this survey worth?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Scale, not inference. It's a non-probability sample that reached people along my networks; no response rate can be computed and none is claimed; no test of significance is run, and nothing is inferred to a population. I use it to set what organisations say about trust beside what the 117 arrangements show binds them (3.6; 5.3).

examiner_questions.question: 89 of 119 say trust is important. Doesn't that contradict your finding that trust doesn't bind?
examiner_questions.model_answer: No, it sits beside it. The survey records what people say matters; the arrangements show what actually held them. And among the 45 who said how they build trust, formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support were named beside joint planning. Saying trust matters and relying on outside binders aren't in conflict (5.3).

examiner_questions.question: Why do companies that don't collaborate answer questions meant for those that do?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Because the form didn't apply the draft's skip. I report the answers as they stand: of the 48 who rated success, 12 don't collaborate now. I read those as past or expected collaboration, and I say the challenges item can't tell a challenge met in an earlier attempt from one that's expected (3.6).

examiner_questions.question: Could your interviewees be among the respondents?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Possibly. The link went to the interview participants while they were being interviewed, and the form asked no name, so the overlap can't be counted. The survey isn't a sample independent of the interviews, and I say so (3.6).

examiner_questions.question: A kappa of 1.00 looks too good to be true.
examiner_questions.model_answer: It's high partly because the codebook was drawn up from these same 39 answers in the first coding, which makes agreement easier in so short a set. The second coding was blind, from the codebook and the answers alone, and I report the agreement with that limit (3.6).

examiner_questions.question: Doesn't this just show that neutral lockers are better lockers?
examiner_questions.model_answer: It might. The networks weren't matched on quality, price or terms, because no public measure of quality was found. The same-carrier check holds the carrier fixed but not the network. So it shows a difference by owner class, not cause, and I say so in M.1 and 3.7.

examiner_questions.question: Twenty-six ownership periods is a tiny sample.
examiner_questions.model_answer: It is, which is why I ran no regression and rest the result on a permutation test that counts each ownership period once: 46.0 per cent against 21.3, p = .008. The pair-level Fisher tests point the same way, but the pairs aren't independent, since one network serves several carriers, so those p-values are indicative only (5.2; M.1).

examiner_questions.question: Does this test your claim that use falls as the holder's market commonality with each carrier rises?
examiner_questions.model_answer: No. Market commonality is coded by the holder's class, not measured pair by pair. The result is consistent with that gradient but doesn't test it, and I say so (M.1; 3.7).

examiner_questions.question: What evidence is there that a sale changes who delivers?
examiner_questions.model_answer: It rests on two changes of owner, each read both ways. When the ex-A1 stations went to Austrian Post, GLS stopped delivering, but Austrian Post wouldn't say which cooperations continued, so there may be other causes. De Buren's sale to DHL Group is covered only by a sale-day statement. The myflexbox sale gives a baseline for a later check (M.1).

examiner_questions.question: Could your sources bias the result?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Yes. A main carrier with no source is counted as not delivering, published sources may under-record carriers, and a neutral network that lives by selling access may list its carriers more readily. The count of pairs with evidence, which leaves unsourced carriers out, points the same way (5.2).

appendices.title: The savings scenario: inputs, sources and formulas
appendices.what_it_is: A worked example of what the proposed rule, checking that shared parcel points are neutral, might cost and save in one imaginary council area of 50,000 households, with every input and formula shown.
appendices.why_it_exists: Backs 3.5 (the scenario method: low, central and high values, a worst case, only the increment counted, £7.08 an hour and 0.167 kg CO2e a kilometre) and 6.3 (the central net value of about £262,000; a check costing about £400 to £1,500 a point a year).

key_facts.fact: One notional council area of 50,000 households; a worked example, not a forecast.
Thirteen inputs, each with low, central and high values; eight are assumptions (P, d, r0, r, c, L, dt and N), and s and k are partly assumed.
Time is valued at the Department for Transport's non-work value and car emissions at the government's average-car factor.
Central case: 280,000 failed first attempts, 84,000 depot trips, 33,600 trips avoided, 28,000 hours saved.
Central case money: time worth £198,240, carrier saving £105,840, check cost £42,000 (60 points at £700), net £262,080 a year.
Low case net −£12,000; stress case (low benefits, high check cost) −£150,000 a year; high case net £1,719,000.
CO2 saved is 28.1 tonnes in the central case and 243.2 in the high; it is reported, not priced.
Only the increment over today's redirection is counted: trips avoided equal depot trips times (r minus r0).
Households without a car (23.3%) account for about 7,829 of the central avoided trips and about 9,134 hours.
For a carrier, the expected cost per parcel is £1.82 at the door against £0.45 to £0.95 at a neutral point.
The check cost per point is built from Charnwood Borough Council's officer cost of £306.51 to £423.55 per licence plus about 24 test parcels at about £4.
The result turns on two inputs: the share of failures redirected (r) and the time saved per trip (dt).

examiner_questions.question: Most of your inputs are assumptions. What is this scenario worth?
examiner_questions.model_answer: It shows the order of magnitude and which inputs drive it, the share redirected and the time saved, and nothing more. Eight of the thirteen inputs are assumptions and I say so; the UK publishes no official first-attempt failure rate and I found no UK data on depot trips. The proper test is the matched-streets design I propose for further research (N.5).

examiner_questions.question: Couldn't the rule lose money?
examiner_questions.model_answer: Yes. In the low case it adds nothing and the council is £12,000 down; in the stress case, low benefits with 100 points checked at £1,500 each, it's £150,000 down a year. The central case is about £262,000 net. I show all of them (N.3; 6.3).

examiner_questions.question: Why don't you price the carbon?
examiner_questions.model_answer: I report it, 28.1 tonnes a year in the central case, but I don't price it, so the net figure is only residents' time and carriers' savings minus the cost of checking (N.2, N.3).

examiner_questions.question: Aren't you counting redirection that already happens?
examiner_questions.model_answer: No. Only the increment counts: trips avoided are depot trips times r minus r0, the share redirected under the rule minus the share already redirected today (N.2).

examiner_questions.question: Lockers can be worse than the doorstep if people drive to them.
examiner_questions.model_answer: They can, as Niemeijer and Buijs found, which is why the rule is limited to shared points in towns within a five-minute walk (N.5).

quiz.q: How many households does the notional council area have?
quiz.explanation: 50,000. 28,000 is the hours saved and 33,600 the trips avoided in the central case.

quiz.q: What is the central net value a year?
quiz.explanation: £262,080 (6.3 says about £262,000). £198,240 is the value of time, £105,840 the carrier saving, £1,719,000 the high case.

quiz.q: At what value is residents' time costed?
quiz.explanation: £7.08, the DfT value for non-work time. 0.167 is the emissions factor in kg CO2e per km; £1.35 the central carrier saving per redelivery.

quiz.q: How many of the thirteen inputs are assumptions?
quiz.explanation: Eight (P, d, r0, r, c, L, dt, N); s and k are partly assumed.

quiz.q: What is the stress case?
quiz.explanation: Low benefits with high check cost: −£150,000. −£12,000 is the low case; £42,000 the central check cost.

quiz.q: How many depot trips are avoided in the central case?
quiz.explanation: 33,600. 84,000 is all depot trips, 280,000 the failed first attempts, 28,000 the hours saved.

quiz.q: What does the check cost per point a year, across the three cases?
quiz.explanation: £400 low, £700 central, £1,500 high. £306.51 to £423.55 is Charnwood's officer cost per licence that it is built from.
